answer.rationale: Timeline is the strongest signal available: the release landed ~2h ago and write-path p99 began climbing ~90m ago, which is consistent with release-induced regression, though correlation is not causation — peak settlement load alone could explain a write-path degradation, and both could be compounding. memory_b1 records a rollback that cleanly cleared a comparable spike, so I want the original record to check whether that incident also occurred under heavy write load or only under light traffic; a rollback validated only in a quiet window is weaker evidence here. memory_b6 records staged gating catching regressions within an hour via canary cohorts; I want the source to see whether this release actually went through that gating, because if it did and canaries were clean, the release is a less likely cause and I should not spend my single intervention on it. Regional failover is explicitly ruled out by memory_b2's own caveat: it restored latency but opened a 40-minute replication gap and lost writes, and writes are hot right now — that directly violates the do-not-lose-customer-writes objective, so it is off the table regardless of its latency appeal. add_capacity (memory_b3) worked pre-emptively before a known peak, not as a mid-incident remedy against a 90-minute climb, and provisioning lag likely exceeds the incident window. route_read_replicas (memory_b5) relieved the primary of read load, but the reported symptom is write-path p99 during settlement peak, where read offload may buy little. enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) contains an external dependency failure; nothing here indicates a partner is failing, and failing fast would shed settlement writes we are trying to protect. So rollback is the best-supported single move, but I am running it as a small guarded test — roll back a limited cohort first and watch write-path p99 on that cohort against the unrolled-back baseline. This gives a causal read rather than a correlational one, and if latency is load-driven rather than release-driven, I learn that without having spent the window on a full fleet-wide change during peak settlement. Downstream risk flagged: rolling back mid-settlement can strand in-flight writes or create incompatibility between records written under the new build and the prior build's handling of them; the guarded scope plus draining in-flight writes before cutting each cohort is the mitigation, and I will not broaden until write-integrity checks are clean on the canary.
